title: WHAT IF A STAR 350x THE SUN
SWALLOWED YOU?

sets.bigstar: A giant star close up. far: deep-navy SpaceBackdrop with sparse stars; mid: a huge red-orange star filling most of the frame with slow boiling convection cells (darker orange blotches drifting) and a soft dusty red halo, 4 px outline on its limb, pale rim light; setp.t 0..1 = the star slowly pulses and the cells drift; setp.glow 'red'|'gold'|'white' tints the halo; setp.dust 0..1 = brown dust shells thicken around it.
sets.binary: Two stars orbiting. Deep-navy bg, thin cream orbit ellipse; centre: a huge red-orange giant star (about 40% of frame height) with soft halo; a tiny bright yellow star on the ellipse; setp.t 0..1 = tiny star travels around the ellipse; setp.close 0..1 = the ellipse shrinks and the tiny star dips toward the giant's surface; setp.trail 0|1 = a gold trail follows the tiny star.
sets.inside: Inside the giant's atmosphere. A full-frame swirl of orange, red and amber gas clouds drifting slowly, thick and soupy, with faint glowing streaks; one tiny bright yellow star dot with a gold spiral trail; setp.t 0..1 = the tiny star spirals inward toward the centre (a bright hot glow); setp.heat 0..1 = the gas brightens toward white-gold; setp.drag 0..1 = the spiral trail tightens.
sets.scale: Top-down Solar System scale. Deep-navy bg; a tiny yellow Sun at centre with thin cream rings for Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars drawn as small coloured dots; a huge translucent red-orange disc (the giant star) centred on the Sun; setp.t 0..1 = the red disc grows from Sun-sized to 350x (it swallows the inner rings one by one and passes Mars); setp.mark 0|1 = a pulsing cyan ring on Earth; setp.zoom 0..1 = camera zooms out.
sets.andromeda: The Andromeda galaxy. Deep-navy bg; a tilted spiral galaxy with a bright cream-white core, blue-white arms, dark brown dust lanes and a small fuzzy companion galaxy; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera push toward the galaxy's lower-right outskirts; setp.box 0..1 = a white square outline draws around one tiny bright dot at the outskirts; setp.glow 0|1 = the dot pulses.
sets.curve: A light curve chart. Deep-navy bg; a dark chart panel with cream axes and faint grid; a gold line: flat, then a slow rise, then a huge spike, then a long slow fade; setp.t 0..1 = the line draws on from left to right; setp.phase 'quiet'|'rise'|'spike'|'fade' = a labelled vertical band highlights that part of the line; setp.zoom 0..1 = zoom into the spike.
sets.scope: A space telescope in deep space. far: SpaceBackdrop; mid: a Webb-style telescope with a hexagon-segment gold mirror, a flat layered silver sunshield and a small body, 4 px outline, pale rim light; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.look 0..1 = a faint cyan cone widens from the mirror toward the sky; setp.blink 0|1 = a camera flash.
sets.lab: A bright astronomers' control room. far: wall of dark screens with soft cream charts and a world map; mid: a desk with two laptops, a coffee mug and a sticky note; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim; setp.alert 0..1 = a screen flashes amber with a warning triangle; setp.ok 1 = screens turn green.
sets.timeline: A horizontal dated timeline. Deep-navy bg; a cream line with year ticks 2018 2023 2024 2025; setp.t 0..1 = a gold marker slides left to right across the line; setp.pins 0..4 = round pins pop up in order (2018, 2023, 2024, 2025); setp.glow 'gold'|'red'.
sets.bowl: A kitchen table in a dark room. near: a wooden table plane with pale rim; mid: a big white bowl of thick orange soup with steam; a silver spoon; setp.t 0..1 = the spoon drags slowly through the soup in a widening swirl; setp.steam 0..1 = steam rising.
sets.blast: A star blowing off its outer layers. Deep-navy bg; centre: a bright white-gold star core; a ring of orange gas expanding outward, brighter at the top and bottom (poles) and held back around the middle by a brown dust belt; setp.t 0..1 = the gas shell expands; setp.flash 0..1 = a white flash at the start; setp.dust 0..1 = dust belt thickness.
sets.core: The centre of a giant star. Full-frame hot white-gold glow fading to orange at the edges, dense swirling gas; setp.t 0..1 = a tiny yellow star dot sinks into the glow and is swallowed (it fades in a bright pulse); setp.shock 0..1 = a ring shock wave radiates outward.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.
sets.roman: Sky survey. Deep-navy bg; a huge dark grid of the sky with many tiny faint stars; a sweeping cyan scan band; small gold sparks flash up at random spots; setp.t 0..1 = the scan band sweeps; setp.sparks 0..1 = more gold sparks appear.

props.starbig: Icon of a giant star: a big red-orange disc with soft glow, darker blotches and a 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.starsmall: Icon of a small star: a bright yellow round disc with a soft glow and 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.spoon: A silver spoon with a dark 4 px outline, tilted; pp.s scale.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: You are a small star. And a giant star is swallowing you.
It weighs seven Suns, and it is three hundred fifty times wider.
This really happened. Astronomers watched it. The paper came out yesterday.
It is two and a half million light-years away, in Andromeda.
film.dir: steady; stress 'two and a half million'

film.vo: So what if you rode the small star all the way down?
Here are the rules.
You are Little Bao. A star a bit smaller than our Sun.
Your friend is Big Bao. Big is the polite word.
You bring nothing. You are a star. You are the luggage.
You do not steer. Physics steers. Physics is not chatty.
The trip takes about seven years. Pack snacks.
First, meet the giant you are about to visit.
Big Bao is a red giant. A very, very old star, puffed up.
It weighs about seven Suns.
It is three hundred fifty times wider than the Sun.
Put it where our Sun is, and its surface would pass Mars.
Earth would be inside it. Along with everything you have ever met.
It is also eighteen thousand times brighter than the Sun.
Next to it, you are a pebble with a glow.
And you weigh about seventy percent of the Sun.
That is the first time anyone has ever measured you.
Scientists found your weight by doing their sums on the dust.
You two had been circling quietly for ages. Millennia, even.
Then your orbit dipped, just a little, and everything changed.
Picture a spoon in thick soup.
Drag it through, and the soup pushes back.
That is you. The giant's outer layers are the soup.
In twenty eighteen your orbit starts brushing its outer atmosphere.
Drag. Slow, patient drag. Your orbit starts to shrink.
And the system begins to glow, very slowly, a little brighter.
Friction turns your orbital energy into light.
A star's version of rubbing your hands to warm them.
Nobody on Earth knows yet. But some telescopes are already looking.
In February twenty twenty-three, NASA's NEOWISE flags something odd.
Before twenty eighteen, the star was steady. Now it is not.
They keep watching. Which is the whole point of this story.
By September twenty twenty-four, a survey sees dust pouring off it.
You are leaking material, and it is getting crowded.
Now the lap count. A lap is one trip round the giant.
Lap one. You skim the atmosphere. Everything is fine.
Lap three. You are lower. The soup is thicker.
Lap five. The gas around you glows orange.
Each lap takes about a year. Each lap gets tighter.
Other star mergers took thousands of laps to happen.
Yours? About seven. Hold on to your halo.
The giant's gas drags you in like quicksand made of fire.
Lap six. You are almost at the centre.
In July twenty twenty-five, NASA's SPHEREx sees it fade in visible light.
And brighten in infrared. That swap is a loud alarm bell.
Dust is hiding the star's light. Something big is coming.
The astronomers do not know when. You know. It is lap seven.
You touch the giant's surface, and the final plunge begins.
Down you go through the gas, faster and faster.
Above you, the whole star lights up.
Then, on the seventeenth of October twenty twenty-five, it erupts.
A flash that fills the sky of a galaxy.
In under a month, it brightens about a hundred times.
Someone spots it first. An amateur astronomer, with a flash of luck.
The team had been watching that very spot for years.
Nobody expected a bang in their lifetime. These stars stay calm for ages.
Luck. Patience. And a spreadsheet that never blinked.
Now, the race. Every telescope on call wants a look.
The Zwicky Transient Facility confirms it on the seventeenth.
In November, NASA's Swift looks. So does Gemini North, in Hawaii.
Every night, a new spectrum. Every spectrum, a new clue.
They all say the same thing: a smaller star fell into a giant.
But did you escape, or did you merge? Nobody knows yet.
Some pairs survive this dance. They end up in tight, shrunken orbits.
So the telescopes need one more clue. A big one.
Enter the James Webb Space Telescope.
It wants to look at the dust the giant shed over centuries.
Dust holds the answer. How much dust, how much gas, how much star.
The date is the twenty-fourth of December. Christmas Eve.
That is forty-seven days after the peak.
The earliest anyone has ever followed up a merger like this.
What did Webb see? A tiny red-and-white dot, wrapped in dust.
The scientists ran their computer models over and over.
One model matched Webb's picture of the dust perfectly.
The model said you had enough energy left to flee.
But a deeper check said no.
You were dragged into the giant's core.
A Columbia scientist said: almost like a bomb inside a living star.
And you? You become part of the giant. One star, instead of two.
The blast threw off about a tenth of the giant's gas.
It flew away at roughly ten times escape speed.
Up and down it flew free. Old dust held back the middle.
The result looks a bit like a dusty hourglass in the sky.
You. A star. Gone, in seven years.
So why does this one matter?
This is called common envelope evolution.
It is how many tight pairs of stars get made.
Some of those pairs later become neutron stars. Or black holes.
Some send out ripples in space itself. Gravitational waves.
Until now, astronomers had to work backwards from old wreckage.
With you, they watched it live, before, during and after.
And it is not over. Bao's fate is still a mystery.
Dust hides the new star. It may take years, even decades, to settle.
Soon there will be more. NASA's Roman telescope starts its surveys.
The lead author expects a large influx of similar discoveries.
Remember the first line? A small star, swallowed by a giant.
Now you know how a telescope, a spreadsheet and luck watched it happen.
Tomorrow: what if the Moon vanished for one night?
Would you ride the small star or the giant? Tell me below.

short.vo: You are a small star. A giant star is swallowing you.
It is three hundred fifty times wider than the Sun.
Its surface would reach past Mars.
You touch it, and the plunge begins.
It takes just seven laps, about seven years.
Other mergers took thousands of laps.
Then, on seventeen October twenty twenty-five, it erupts.
A hundred times brighter in under a month.
Webb caught the aftermath, forty-seven days later.
The small star did not escape. It was dragged to the core.
Astronomers watched a stellar merger from start to finish. A first.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: what if the Moon vanished?
